newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Sterling tries tentative rally in quiet Asia trade.
newsitem.headline: Sterling tries tentative rally in quiet Asia trade.

text.p: Sterling was ending Asian trading on a firmer note on Friday as traders digested the enormity of Labour's landslide victory in the British general election.
"A Labour victory was priced in, but what wasn't in the price -- or even the market psychology -- was the huge extent of the victory," a trader at an Australian house in Singapore said.
"Sterling is trying a tentative rally at the moment, but there's no real volume behind it. In fact, trade has been quiet all day," he said.
At 0447 GMT, Labour had 416 parliamentary seats and the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) estimated it would have a majority over the Conservatives of some 179 seats.
The trader said the market had priced in a Labour majority of anywhere between 50 to 80 seats.
Sterling was quoted at 2.8010/20 marks at 0455 GMT while cable was quoted at 1.6250/60 dollars.
Sterling had initially rallied to 2.8010/20 and 1.6290/6300 respectively just after exit polls had predicted a Labour win.
But then some selling kicked in as traders became concerned that the extent of the win could give Labour carte-blanche to enact whatever legislation it liked.
"The rally on the exit polls was a knee-jerk reaction, one of relief that we weren't going to get a hung parliament," a trader at a European bank in Singapore said.
He added, "Because it's such a large majority it means Labour can do what they like. But what does that mean? No-one really knows."
But the head of trading at a U.S. bank in Singapore said these fears were overdone.
"Some people are scared that the left wing (of the Labour Party) will rear its ugly head -- I doubt it," he said.
He said he expected sterling to remain within its recent trading range against the mark of 2.7800/8250 for the time being.
"I think you should buy sterling on the dips because of the interest rate scenario. And you can't ignore such fundamentals as economic growth and inflation," he added.
Bank base rates in the U.K. stand at six percent, but Bank of England Governor Eddie George has been pressing for a rise of 1/4 point for some months now.
"I get the impression Blair is more conservative than Major," the head of added.
He said he was encouraged by comments made by Gordon Brown to Reuters Financial Television early on Friday.
Brown told RFTV a Labour government would stick to an inflation target of 2.5 percent and would set monetary policy to meet it.
"I take those as bullish comments and have bought some sterling," the trader said.
The head of Treasury at another European bank said he still favoured the scenario of an upward move in U.K. interest rates pretty soon.

He noted that futures markets have priced in a rise of 1/2 point over the next few months and said he was still keen to find out definitively whether or not the new Labour Chancellor of the Exchequer -- expected to be Gordon Brown -- would be meeting the Bank of England's George on May 7 next week.
Earlier the BBC said Brown was expecting to honour the usual monthly meeting held between the Chancellor and the Governor.
-- Singapore newsroom (65) 870-3080
